# Chorus-Wave Polarization (SVD)

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** Multi-channel SVD wave analysis — recovering a wave's propagation direction and polarization from a *single* spacecraft's three-component magnetic field.
**Chapter:** [8 — Multi-Channel Analysis](../chap8.qmd)

---

## Background

**Whistler-mode chorus** is one of the most important wave modes in near-Earth space: these rising-tone electromagnetic emissions accelerate radiation-belt electrons to relativistic energies and scatter them into the atmosphere to light up the diffuse aurora. The Japanese **Arase (ERG)** satellite records the three-component magnetic field $\mathbf{B}(t)$ of these waves with its Waveform Capture (WFC) receiver.

But a single spacecraft is one moving point: it measures a time series, not a spatial pattern, so it cannot directly see the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$. The trick is to bring in **Maxwell's equations**. In Fourier space $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ becomes $\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{B}}(\omega)=0$ — the wave vector must be **perpendicular to the magnetic fluctuation**. That single parameter-free constraint, applied across a spectrum of measurements, is enough to reconstruct the propagation direction and the full polarization state.

## Key idea

Form the $3\times3$ **spectral matrix** from the three field components,

$$
\hat{S}_{ij}(\omega) = \langle \hat{B}_i(\omega)\,\hat{B}_j^*(\omega)\rangle,
$$

averaged over neighbouring times and frequencies. The wave vector is the direction $\boldsymbol{\kappa}$ that best satisfies $\hat{S}\boldsymbol{\kappa}=0$. [Santolík et al. (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2000RS002523) stack the real and imaginary parts of $\hat S$ into a $6\times3$ matrix $A$ and solve it by **singular value decomposition**, $A = U\,W\,V^{\mathsf T}$. The three singular values $W_0 \ge W_1 \ge W_2$ then read out the wave's geometry directly:

- **wave-normal angle** — the angle between $\boldsymbol{\kappa}$ (from the smallest singular vector) and the background field $\mathbf{B}_0$;
- **planarity** $F = 1 - \sqrt{W_2/W_0}$ — whether the fluctuations lie in a single plane (one common $\mathbf{k}$);
- **ellipticity** $W_1/W_0$ — linear vs circular polarization;
- **compressibility** and **degree of polarization** — how transverse and how coherent the wave is.

## Code

```python
import numpy as np
import bottleneck as bn

# coef: short-time Fourier coefficients of the 3 magnetic components, shape (freq, time, 3)
# --- spectral matrix S_ij = <B_i B_j*>, smoothed over frequency and time ---
spec = np.einsum('fti,ftj->ftij', coef, coef.conj())
spec = bn.move_mean(spec, window=freq_window, min_count=1, axis=0)
spec = bn.move_mean(spec, window=time_window, min_count=1, axis=1)

# --- Santolik 6x3 augmented matrix [Re S ; Im S], then SVD at every (f, t) ---
spec_63 = np.concatenate([spec.real, spec.imag], axis=-2)
u, s, vh = np.linalg.svd(spec_63, full_matrices=False)   # s: three singular values, descending

planarity         = 1 - np.sqrt(s[:, :, 2] / s[:, :, 0])   # 1 = one common wave vector
ellipticity_along_k = s[:, :, 1] / s[:, :, 0]              # 0 = linear, 1 = circular
kappa = vh[:, :, 2, :]                                     # wave-normal direction (smallest sing. vector)
wave_normal_angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.abs(kappa @ b0_hat)))   # angle to background field
```

## Result

<div class="gallery-result">
![Whistler-mode chorus observed by Arase/ERG-WFC on 2017-03-31. Top: the three-component magnetic waveform. Below it, the power spectrogram shows discrete rising-tone chorus elements near 1–2 kHz, and the SVD spectral-matrix analysis returns, frequency-by-frequency, the compressibility, ellipticity (along k and along B), wave-normal angle, coherency, planarity, and degree of polarization.](../Figure/figure_svd_erg.png)
</div>

The stack of panels is a complete wave-mode diagnosis of the chorus emissions from a single spacecraft. Wherever the spectrogram lights up with a chorus element, the SVD panels agree on a consistent story: **low compressibility** (blue — the fluctuations are transverse, not compressional), **ellipticity near 1** and a **right-handed sense along $\mathbf{B}$** (circular polarization), a **small wave-normal angle** (blue — the waves propagate nearly *along* the background field), and **high planarity, coherency, and degree of polarization** (red — a single, well-defined, highly polarized wave vector). That combination — transverse, right-hand circular, quasi-field-aligned, coherent — is the textbook signature of **whistler-mode chorus**, read straight off the singular values. One receiver, three components, and Maxwell's $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ turn a time series into the full propagation geometry.
